text: Antivirus and EDR solve overlapping problems in very different ways, and the difference is the backbone of modern endpoint security. In this lesson we'll trace how endpoint protection evolved from matching known malware signatures to watching behavior in real time, and why today's SOCs treat EDR as a core data source rather than a background utility.

Traditional antivirus works by comparing files against a database of known malware signatures — hashes and byte patterns. Scan a file, check its hash or pattern against that list, flag a match. It's fast, cheap, and effective against malware that's already been seen and catalogued somewhere. Its blind spot is anything that hasn't been catalogued yet: zero-day malware with no existing signature, polymorphic malware that rewrites its own code to produce a new hash on every infection, and fileless attacks that never write a recognizable file to disk at all.

EDR takes a completely different approach. Instead of asking whether a static file matches a known bad hash, an EDR agent continuously streams telemetry off the endpoint — every process that starts, which process launched it, command-line arguments, network connections, file and registry changes. It builds a process tree showing those parent-child relationships, so analysts aren't looking at one suspicious file, they're looking at a sequence of behavior across the whole chain of events.

That behavioral view is also why EDR can do more than detect. A traditional antivirus response is quarantine or delete the file. EDR gives an analyst the ability to isolate a compromised host from the network while leaving it running for investigation, kill a malicious process remotely, and pull a forensic timeline — response, not just detection, is the second half of the name.

Picture a phishing attachment whose macro launches PowerShell with an obfuscated, encoded command that downloads a payload straight into memory — nothing is ever written to disk as a file. Signature-based antivirus has nothing to scan and raises no alert. EDR sees Word spawn PowerShell with suspicious encoded arguments, then that process making an outbound connection to an unfamiliar address, and flags the whole process tree within minutes.

That's the real shift: from matching known artifacts to watching behavior and being able to act on it. It's why EDR telemetry now feeds SIEM and XDR platforms and anchors modern threat hunting across whole fleets of machines, not just one at a time. Next, we'll look at one real implementation of that model: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
